blocks.content: Most concurrency bugs are not caused by threads doing something wrong in isolation. They are caused by two or more threads sharing one piece of mutable state and stepping on each other while updating it.

There is a class of object that sidesteps this entire problem by construction. An object that can never change after it is built simply has nothing for two threads to race over. No matter how many threads read it, at the same instant, from different cores, they all see the exact same value forever.

This lesson is about that idea in a very practical sense, not as a theoretical curiosity. We will look at why shared mutable state is the actual root cause behind most race conditions, how to build a class that is genuinely immutable rather than just accidentally hard to modify, and where this strategy is worth its performance cost and where it is not.
By the end, you should be able to look at a class and tell, with confidence, whether it is thread safe simply by checking whether it can ever change after construction.
An immutable object cannot have a race condition, because a race condition requires two threads to disagree about a value that is changing, and an immutable object never changes.
1. Shared Mutable State Is the Root of Almost Every Concurrency Bug
blocks.text: 1. Shared Mutable State Is the Root of Almost Every Concurrency Bug

blocks.content: When people describe concurrency bugs, they use words like race condition, data race, or lost update. Underneath all of those names is the same shape of problem.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499610440-387117834.png
blocks.alt: Three ingredients, shared state, mutable state, and no synchronization, combining into a race condition that produces an unpredictable result

blocks.content: The three ingredients of a race condition
blocks.text: The three ingredients of a race condition

blocks.content: ["State that is shared, meaning more than one thread can see and touch it","State that is mutable, meaning its value can change after it was created","No coordination, meaning nothing forces the threads to take turns safely"]
items: State that is shared, meaning more than one thread can see and touch it
State that is mutable, meaning its value can change after it was created
No coordination, meaning nothing forces the threads to take turns safely

blocks.content: Remove any one of those three ingredients and the bug disappears. Locks and synchronized blocks attack the third ingredient, coordination. Immutability attacks the second ingredient directly, mutability, and it removes the problem instead of managing it.
A concrete way to see the difference
blocks.text: A concrete way to see the difference

blocks.content: A bank balance that two threads can both read and write is shared and mutable, so it needs coordination. A tax rate constant loaded once at startup is shared but never mutable, so it never needs any coordination at all, no matter how many threads read it.
This is the entire insight behind reaching for immutability first. If the second ingredient is missing, the third one becomes unnecessary, and an entire class of bug simply cannot occur.

blocks.title: Why this angle matters
blocks.content: Locks are a way to make mutation safe. Immutability is a way to make mutation unnecessary. The second option is strictly simpler when it is available, because there is no coordination logic left to get wrong.
2. What Actually Makes a Class Immutable
blocks.text: 2. What Actually Makes a Class Immutable

blocks.content: A class is not immutable just because you feel like you will not change it. It is immutable only if the compiler and the runtime make change impossible, for every thread, in every situation.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499612380-912926322.png
blocks.alt: Four rules feeding into a genuinely immutable class, all fields final, no setter methods, fully built inside the constructor, and no leaked reference to a mutable field

blocks.content: The four rules
blocks.text: The four rules

blocks.content: ["Every field is declared final, and assigned exactly once, inside the constructor","No method exists that sets a field after construction, no setters of any kind","The class itself is final, or otherwise cannot be subtly subclassed into a mutable variant","Any field that is itself a mutable type, like a list, a date, or an array, is defensively copied on the way in and on the way out"]
items: Every field is declared final, and assigned exactly once, inside the constructor
No method exists that sets a field after construction, no setters of any kind
The class itself is final, or otherwise cannot be subtly subclassed into a mutable variant
Any field that is itself a mutable type, like a list, a date, or an array, is defensively copied on the way in and on the way out

blocks.content: The first three rules are usually easy to remember. The fourth one is where most so called immutable classes quietly fail, and it deserves its own section next.
3. The Defensive Copy Problem
blocks.text: 3. The Defensive Copy Problem

blocks.content: Marking a field final only stops you from reassigning the reference. It does not stop anyone from reaching through that reference and mutating the object it points to.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499613864-521406062.png
blocks.alt: Two separate leaks, a constructor that stores the caller list directly and a getter that returns the internal field directly, both ending in broken immutability

blocks.content: Where a leak sneaks in
blocks.text: Where a leak sneaks in

blocks.content: If your constructor stores a reference to a caller supplied list without copying it, the caller still holds their own reference to that same list. They can mutate it after construction, and your supposedly immutable object changes along with it.
Where a second leak sneaks in
blocks.text: Where a second leak sneaks in

blocks.content: If a getter returns your internal mutable field directly, any caller of that getter can mutate the object through the returned reference, from any thread, at any time.

{"headers":["Leak point","What goes wrong","The fix"],"rows":[["Constructor stores caller reference directly","Caller mutates their original object after construction","Copy the mutable input inside the constructor"],["Getter returns internal field directly","Caller mutates the internal state through the returned reference","Return a copy, or an unmodifiable view, from the getter"],["Field is an array","Arrays are always mutable in place, even if final","Clone the array on the way in and on the way out"]]}

blocks.title: A useful test
blocks.content: Ask yourself, after this object is constructed, is there any reference anywhere in the program, held by anyone, that can be used to change a field. If the answer is yes, the class is not actually immutable, no matter how it looks.
4. A Mutable Class With a Real Race Condition
blocks.text: 4. A Mutable Class With a Real Race Condition

blocks.content: The clearest way to see why this matters is to watch a mutable class fail under concurrent access, then fix it by making it immutable instead of by adding locks.
The mutable version
blocks.text: The mutable version

blocks.content: Here is an ordinary looking coordinate class with setters. Nothing about it looks dangerous when you read it top to bottom on its own.
The bug in action
blocks.text: The bug in action

blocks.content: Now put this object where two threads can reach it at the same time. One thread repeatedly moves the point along a diagonal, another thread repeatedly reads and prints it.

codes.python:
import threading

shared = MutablePoint(0, 0)

def mover():
    for i in range(1_000_000):
        shared.set_x(i)
        shared.set_y(i)

def reader():
    for i in range(1_000_000):
        snapshot = shared.describe()
        # Even with the GIL, this interleaving can print an x and y
        # that were never set together, since set_x and set_y are
        # two separate operations with a gap between them.
        print(snapshot)

threading.Thread(target=mover).start()
threading.Thread(target=reader).start()

blocks.title: What actually happens
blocks.text: The reader thread can call describe partway through the mover thread updating x and setting y. It reads a fresh x and a stale y, or vice versa, and hands back a coordinate pair that was never a real position the point ever held. No exception is thrown. No error is logged. The bug just quietly corrupts data.

blocks.content: 5. The Same Class Made Properly Immutable
blocks.text: 5. The Same Class Made Properly Immutable

blocks.content: Now build the same idea again, but this time with every field final, no setters at all, and a method that returns a new object instead of mutating the existing one.

Notice what disappeared compared to the mutable version. There is no setX, no setY, no window between two separate writes for a reader to catch mid update. The object is either the old point or the new point, and there is nothing in between for a reader to observe.
6. Proving the Immutable Version Cannot Be Corrupted
blocks.text: 6. Proving the Immutable Version Cannot Be Corrupted

blocks.content: Run the exact same two threads against the immutable version, one thread repeatedly building new points along the diagonal and swapping a shared reference, another repeatedly reading whatever the current reference points to.

codes.python:
import threading

shared = ImmutablePoint(0, 0)

def mover():
    global shared
    for i in range(1_000_000):
        shared = shared.move_to(i, i)

def reader():
    for i in range(1_000_000):
        snapshot = shared
        # snapshot is a fully built, frozen object the instant it is
        # assigned, so describe on it can never see a half updated pair.
        print(snapshot.describe())

threading.Thread(target=mover).start()
threading.Thread(target=reader).start()

blocks.content: The reference itself can still be swapped out from under the reader, that part is unavoidable whenever state changes over time. But the object each swap points to is always a complete, internally consistent point. There is no in between state for any thread to ever observe, because the object was fully built before any other thread could see it at all.

blocks.title: What changed and what did not
blocks.content: Both versions still have state that changes over time, the position genuinely moves in both examples. The difference is that the mutable version changes an existing object in place, exposing a half updated state to other threads, while the immutable version always swaps in a brand new, fully formed object.
7. Defensive Copies for Fields That Are Themselves Mutable
blocks.text: 7. Defensive Copies for Fields That Are Themselves Mutable

blocks.content: Coordinates are simple because ints cannot be mutated in place. Most real classes are not that lucky, they hold lists, maps, dates, or other objects that are mutable by nature.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499615645-695626601.png
blocks.alt: Constructor copies the caller supplied list in, stores it as a private internal list, and the getter copies it back out so the caller only ever holds an independent list

blocks.content: An immutable class wrapping a mutable field
blocks.text: An immutable class wrapping a mutable field

blocks.content: Two copies matter here, not one. The constructor copies the caller supplied list so later changes to their list do not leak in, and the getter either returns an already unmodifiable view or a fresh copy so callers cannot mutate the internal state on the way out.
8. The Performance Tradeoff of Immutability
blocks.text: 8. The Performance Tradeoff of Immutability

blocks.content: Immutability is not free. Every logical change now allocates a brand new object instead of updating a field in place, and that has a real cost in allocation pressure and garbage collection work.
Where the cost shows up
blocks.text: Where the cost shows up

blocks.content: ["A small object like a point or a money value is cheap to reallocate constantly, the cost is close to negligible","A large collection rebuilt on every single element change can become genuinely expensive if done naively","Persistent, structure sharing data structures exist specifically to make large immutable collections cheap to update, by reusing most of the old structure instead of copying it all"]
items: A small object like a point or a money value is cheap to reallocate constantly, the cost is close to negligible
A large collection rebuilt on every single element change can become genuinely expensive if done naively
Persistent, structure sharing data structures exist specifically to make large immutable collections cheap to update, by reusing most of the old structure instead of copying it all

blocks.content: {"pros":["Impossible to have a race condition on the object itself, nothing to synchronize","Safe to share freely across threads, caches, and callers without any copying","Easier to reason about, an immutable object is always in whatever state it started in","No defensive copying needed for callers, since it can never change under them either"],"cons":["Every change allocates a new object, increasing garbage collector work","Naive immutable updates to large collections can be slow without structure sharing","Can feel unnatural for objects that genuinely represent something that changes very often, like a live counter"]}

In practice, the allocation cost of immutability is usually far cheaper than people assume, and it is almost always cheaper than the cost of debugging a race condition that only shows up under production load.
9. Where Immutability Is Not Practical
blocks.text: 9. Where Immutability Is Not Practical

blocks.content: Immutability is not a universal answer. Some state genuinely needs to be updated in place, often for performance reasons, and forcing it to be immutable would fight the problem rather than solve it.

{"headers":["Situation","Why immutability struggles here","What is used instead"],"rows":[["A counter incremented millions of times per second","Allocating a new object per increment is wasteful","Atomic variables or synchronized mutation"],["A large in memory cache updated frequently","Copying the whole structure per update is too slow without sharing","Concurrent hash maps or persistent structures"],["A connection or file handle representing a live resource","The resource itself is inherently stateful, not a value","Careful lifecycle management with explicit synchronization"],["A UI widget tree that must reflect live user input","Immutable replacement of the whole tree per keystroke can be costly","Localized mutable state with clear ownership"]]}

blocks.title: The real question to ask
blocks.content: Is this thing a value, something that represents a fixed fact like a date or an amount, or is it an identity, something that represents an ongoing, changing process. Values make excellent immutable objects. Identities usually do not.
10. Immutable References Versus Immutable Objects
blocks.text: 10. Immutable References Versus Immutable Objects

blocks.content: It helps to separate two different ideas that get blurred together, whether a variable can be reassigned, and whether the object that variable points to can be internally changed.
Two independent axes
blocks.text: Two independent axes

blocks.content: ["A final or const reference stops reassignment of the variable itself, it says nothing about the object it points to","An immutable object stops internal changes to the object, regardless of how many variables point to it","True thread safety through immutability requires the object to be immutable, a final reference to a mutable object is not enough"]
items: A final or const reference stops reassignment of the variable itself, it says nothing about the object it points to
An immutable object stops internal changes to the object, regardless of how many variables point to it
True thread safety through immutability requires the object to be immutable, a final reference to a mutable object is not enough

blocks.content: A final field holding a mutable ArrayList is a common trap. The reference cannot be reassigned, which feels safe, but any thread with access can still call add or remove on that same list, and the underlying race condition is completely untouched.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494926112-48555668.png
blocks.alt: Two threads safely reading one immutable point on the left, versus two threads corrupting a shared mutable point on the right

blocks.content: 11. A Second Worked Example, Immutable Money
blocks.text: 11. A Second Worked Example, Immutable Money

blocks.content: Coordinates make the bug easy to see, but the same pattern shows up constantly with money, and getting it wrong there is a lot more expensive.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499617838-800148843.png
blocks.alt: Mutable money where both threads read the same balance and write their own update so one deposit is silently lost, versus immutable money where each deposit builds a new object and the winning thread swaps the shared reference

blocks.content: A mutable money class with a hidden bug
blocks.text: A mutable money class with a hidden bug

blocks.content: A mutable balance that supports deposit and withdraw looks completely ordinary, right up until two threads call those methods on the same account at the same time.

When two deposits run at nearly the same moment, both threads can read the same starting value before either write lands, and one of the two deposits is silently lost. The account ends up short, with no error anywhere in the logs.
The immutable equivalent
blocks.text: The immutable equivalent

blocks.content: An immutable Money object never gets updated in place. Every operation returns a brand new, fully formed Money value, so there is no read, modify, write gap for another thread to land inside.

Whichever thread finishes last simply overwrites the shared reference with its own freshly built Money value. Callers must now be careful to apply every update against the latest reference, but each individual Money value is always internally correct, never half written.
12. Common Mistakes When Building Immutable Classes
blocks.text: 12. Common Mistakes When Building Immutable Classes

blocks.content: Most broken immutable classes fail for one of a small handful of repeated reasons, and it is worth naming them plainly.

["Marking fields final but forgetting to defensively copy a mutable field passed into the constructor","Returning an internal mutable field directly from a getter instead of a copy or an unmodifiable view","Leaving the class non final, allowing a subclass to add mutable state or override behavior","Exposing a mutable builder or helper object as a public field instead of keeping it private during construction","Assuming a final reference to a list or map means the collection itself cannot change"]
items: Marking fields final but forgetting to defensively copy a mutable field passed into the constructor
Returning an internal mutable field directly from a getter instead of a copy or an unmodifiable view
Leaving the class non final, allowing a subclass to add mutable state or override behavior
Exposing a mutable builder or helper object as a public field instead of keeping it private during construction
Assuming a final reference to a list or map means the collection itself cannot change

blocks.content: 13. A Quick Checklist Before Calling a Class Immutable
blocks.text: 13. A Quick Checklist Before Calling a Class Immutable

blocks.content: Before trusting a class to be safe across threads simply because it looks immutable, run it through a short checklist.

["Are all fields declared final and set only inside the constructor","Is there truly no method, public or otherwise, that changes a field after construction","Is the class itself final, or otherwise protected from being subclassed into something mutable","Is every mutable constructor argument copied before being stored","Does every getter return either an immutable value, a copy, or an unmodifiable view"]
items: Are all fields declared final and set only inside the constructor
Is there truly no method, public or otherwise, that changes a field after construction
Is the class itself final, or otherwise protected from being subclassed into something mutable
Is every mutable constructor argument copied before being stored
Does every getter return either an immutable value, a copy, or an unmodifiable view

blocks.content: If every answer is yes, the class is genuinely immutable, and it is automatically thread safe with zero synchronization code anywhere.
14. Immutability as the Simplest Concurrency Strategy
blocks.text: 14. Immutability as the Simplest Concurrency Strategy

blocks.content: Every other concurrency tool, locks, atomic operations, concurrent collections, is fundamentally a way to manage change safely when change cannot be avoided. Immutability is different, it removes the need for that management entirely, for the specific piece of state that no longer changes.

That is why experienced engineers reach for immutable objects first, before reaching for a lock. A lock has to be acquired correctly, held for the right duration, and released in every code path, including error paths. An immutable object needs none of that, because there is nothing left to protect.

The practical habit worth building from this lesson is simple. Before adding synchronization to a class that is causing concurrency bugs, first ask whether that class actually needs to be mutable at all. Often the honest answer is no, and the fix is not a better lock, it is removing the mutation altogether.
The cheapest concurrency bug to fix is the one that was never possible in the first place, and immutability is how you buy that guarantee.
